nodes.question: Why is ongoing monitoring of radon emissions necessary?
nodes.answer: Ongoing monitoring is necessary because erosion and geological changes can alter natural radon emission patterns, which poses risks for indoor radon exposure.
nodes.paragraph: Climate change induced geological and soil changes may also affect radon emission patterns (Koike et al., 2015). Thawing permafrost in cold regions can release trapped radon gas from the soil, increasing indoor radon levels in buildings con- structed on or near these areas (World Health Organi- zation, 2009). Land use changes, driven by climate adaptation strategies, can disturb the soil and poten- tially increase radon emissions (Datta et al., 2025). Erosion and other geological changes can alter the natural radon emission patterns, highlighting the need for ongoing monitoring and adaptation of building practices to manage radon risks effectively (Appleton, 2007). Understanding how climate change influences radon concentration in residential houses is essen- tial for developing comprehensive strategies to pro- tect public health (World Health Organization, 2009; Environmental Protection Agency, 2021). As cli- mate change continues to alter environmental condi- tions, it is crucial to integrate climate science, build- ing engineering, and public health efforts to address the dynamic challenges posed by indoor radon. This manuscript discusses the link between climate change parameters and elevated indoor radon levels to enable an urgent call for public health intervention.

nodes.question: Why is post-irradiation examination (PIE) important in nuclear reactor research?
nodes.answer: PIE is important because it measures the performance of nuclear fuels and materials and helps understand their behaviors in the extreme temperature and radiation environments of a nuclear reactor.
nodes.paragraph: Idaho National Laboratory (INL), founded in 1949 as heNational Reactor Testing Station, has the mission of discovering, demonstrating, and securing innova- tive nuclear energy solutions, other clean energyoptions, and critical infrastructure. As part of this mission space, post-irradiation examination (PIE) is performed on nuclear fuels and materials to mea-sure their performance and understand the mate-rial behaviors in the extreme temperature and radiation environments of a nuclear reactor. Traditional PIE activities 6include nondestructive techniques such as visual inspection and pro lom- etry,7,8ultrasonic thickness testing,9 11gamma-(Received April 29, 2024; accepted October 18, 2024; published online December 18, 2024)JOM, Vol. 77, No. 3, 2025 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-24-6970-z/C2112024 Battelle Energy Alliance, under exclusive licence to The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society 1337 emission scanning, 12neutron radiography13, 14and tomography, 15, 16some semi-destructive examina- tions such as ssion-gas sampling, 17as well as destructive examinations involving techniques such as focused ion beam (FIB), scanning electron micro- scope (SEM), transmission electron microscope(TEM), 18 23and thermal property measure- ments,24 26among others.

nodes.question: What is one of the main goals of introducing XCT into the PIE workflow for nuclear materials?
nodes.answer: One of the main goals is to provide a non-destructive means to probe the structure in three dimensions, revealing insights into the effects of irradiation on material structures.
nodes.paragraph: 39The goal of introducing XCT into the PIE work ow for nuclear materials is twofold. First, XCT provides a non-destructive means to probe the structure inthree dimensions, providing the potential to revealinvaluable insights into the effects of irradiation on the evolution of material structures. 40Second, XCT can inform subsequent targeted destructive analy-sis by identifying features of interest for further examination with higher-resolution, smaller eld- of-view (FOV) techniques without having to ran-domly search for desired features, saving time and improving results. The larger FOV of XCT also ensures a region of interest (ROI) is representativeof the larger sample composition. Additionally, realistic internal 3D geometry generated using XCT can be meshed and used as a high- delityinput for fuel performance and other modelingefforts. This paper describes the XCT capabilities at INL and its application to support INL S mission of examining energy materials with an emphasis onPIE capabilities. INSTRUMENTATION AND FACILITY INFORMATION Irradiated Materials Characterization Laboratory (IMCL) Facility IMCL, which began operations in 2015, 41is a Hazard Category-2 Nuclear Facility that can handle highly radioactive materials. It consists of a varietyof tools to enable PIE of irradiated materials forcharacterization of material performance inChuirazzi, Kancharla, and Morankar 1338 extreme reactor environments which contain high temperatures and large radiation elds.

nodes.question: What are gamma rays commonly used for in the context of plants?
nodes.answer: Gamma rays are commonly used as mutagens due to their ease of application, good penetration, reproducibility, high mutation frequency, and fewer disposal problems.
nodes.paragraph: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation, commonly used as mutagens due to their ease of application, good penetration, reproducibility, high mutation frequency, and fewer disposal problems [9]. Gamma rays biologi - cal effect is dependent on their interaction with atoms or molecules in the cell, notably water, which produces free radicals [10]. These radicals can harm or disrupt essen - tial components of plant cells and have been documented to influence the morphology, anatomy, biochemistry, and physiology of plants in different ways depending on the radiation dose [11]. These impacts include changes in the plants cellular structure and metabolism, such as dilata - tion of thylakoid membranes, variation in photosynthesis, modulation of the antioxidant system, and accumulation of phenolic chemicals [12]. Low-dose ionizing irradiation on plants manifests as accelerated cell proliferation, ger - mination rate, cell growth, enzyme activity, stress resist - ance, and crop yields [13]. Gamma irradiation is more effective for improving the qualities and self-life of grains and fruits and can increase genetic diversity for tradi - tional breeding to scrutinize new genotypes with better traits, such as stress tolerance, grain yield, and quality [9].
